title: Acquiring an Established Business: What the Financial Numbers Must Reveal Before You Draft an Offer
excerpt: Evaluating an acquisition target requires looking beyond topline revenue. Discover how earnings quality, tax structures, working capital, and cash flow dictate true deal value.
description: Analyze key business acquisition metrics, including SDE vs EBITDA, working capital, tax structures, and cash flow, before making a purchase offer.

blocks.html:
Starting a brand-new enterprise from scratch is no longer the sole path into business ownership. For an expanding demographic of prospective buyers, the primary opportunity lies in acquiring an existing enterprise—one with an established customer base, trained personnel, operational infrastructure, continuous top-line revenue, and predictable cash flow.

This shift in entrepreneurial strategy is becoming increasingly prominent across the market. In BizBuySell's 2026 market research, 48% of business brokers reported increased activity from Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition buyers and search funds.

Purchasing an established operation provides an immediate head start that could otherwise demand years of organic effort to construct. However, this transition carries a distinct set of operational and financial liabilities. You are buying someone else's history. Before determining what that history is worth, a thorough examination of the financial statements must reveal what you are genuinely acquiring—rather than merely what the seller hopes to highlight.

Topline Revenue Is the Beginning, Not the Final Answer

A target company generating $3 million in annual top-line revenue naturally appears more compelling than one producing $1 million. Yet top-line sales, standing alone, reveal remarkably little about the actual economic reality of the business you will inherit.

To evaluate true financial viability, buyers must investigate the structural movements that occur after top-line revenue enters the business. How much of that income is absorbed by direct labor costs? What portion is allocated to raw materials and supplies? Are gross and operating margins expanding, or are they experiencing steady deterioration over time? Does the company's continuous operation demand heavy capital investments in equipment or inventory? Crucially, how much discretionary cash ultimately remains for the business owner?

Two independent enterprises can report identical gross revenues while exhibiting completely different internal economics. Consequently, one of the first questions an acquisition buyer should ask is not simply: How much does this company sell? Instead, the core inquiry must be: What does this company actually produce from those sales?

Evaluate Historical Financial Trends Over Multiple Periods

Sellers naturally present their companies in the most favorable light possible. A standout fiscal year with record sales may genuinely demonstrate what the enterprise can achieve under optimal conditions. However, a single exceptional period should never serve as the sole foundation for your acquisition decision.

A rigorous review demands analyzing performance trends across several consecutive operating periods. Is gross revenue expanding on a sustainable, predictable trajectory? Are profit margins staying consistent over time? Did payroll expenses rise in step with increased volume, or were staff overstretched? Has underlying profitability demonstrated consistent improvement? Was the most recent year's record volume driven by a single, non-recurring customer order? Were necessary operational or capital expenses intentionally delayed to artificially boost reported profit?

While one outstanding year offers an encouraging snapshot, evaluating financial trends across multiple years provides the comprehensive story required to understand the business you intend to acquire.

Understanding the Critical Differences Between SDE and EBITDA

Listings for smaller closely held businesses frequently highlight Seller's Discretionary Earnings, commonly known as SDE. Middle-market transactions and larger corporate sales are far more likely to center on EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization) or another variant of adjusted corporate earnings. These metrics are fundamental to valuation, but they are by no means interchangeable.

Seller's Discretionary Earnings is generally designed to capture the full economic benefit available to a single owner-operator. To arrive at SDE, financial statements typically add back the total compensation of one full-time owner, along with specific personal or discretionary expenses paid through the business. This distinction raises a fundamental question for any buyer: Are you buying an investment, or are you buying yourself a job?

Consider a business listing that advertises $500,000 in annual SDE. That figure does not imply that a new owner can hire a general manager, step away from daily operations, and passively collect $500,000 per year. A significant portion of that SDE figure reflects direct compensation for the physical and operational work currently performed by the seller. If replacing that seller requires hiring an executive manager at a market rate of $150,000 per year, the baseline economics of your investment change dramatically. Understanding precisely which earnings metric is being presented—and dissecting every specific add-back used to calculate it—is vital before comparing asking prices or market valuation multiples.

Replace the Seller on Paper Prior to Executing an Acquisition

Mapping out the owner's true responsibilities is one of the most effective analytical exercises an acquisition buyer can perform. Document every task, relationship, and duty the current business owner handles on a daily, weekly, and seasonal basis.

While the seller may hold the formal title of President or CEO, closer inspection often reveals that they also perform critical operational tasks, such as:

  • Generating the vast majority of new business and sales leads
  • Managing and retaining the company's highest-value customer accounts
  • Reviewing and approving project pricing and bid proposals
  • Recruiting, hiring, and onboarding frontline employees
  • Estimating project scope and job costs
  • Directing daily operational workflows
  • Maintaining primary relationships with key suppliers and vendors
  • Resolving complex operational problems that no other staff member is equipped to handle

Analyzing what happens when that individual steps away is essential. If you plan to step into those exact roles as an active owner-operator, you must recognize that a substantial share of the business's reported earnings represents direct compensation for your future labor. If your strategy involves hiring management personnel or existing staff to assume those duties, those managerial salary costs must be built into your financial model prior to determining net earnings.

Owner compensation adjustments can cut both ways. If a seller has been taking a salary more than a market replacement salary, the excess portion above market value may legitimately support a positive add-back to earnings. Conversely, if the seller has been taking compensation less than it would cost to replace their work with qualified staff, the necessary financial adjustment moves in the opposite direction. Under those circumstances, the business will prove less profitable under new ownership than its historical income statements suggest.

Determine the True Cash Generation of the Enterprise

While reported accounting net income is an essential benchmark, actual cash flow is what meets payroll obligations, funds operational expansion, services acquisition debt, and delivers a tangible return on invested capital. A company that appears highly profitable on an accrual income statement may still demand substantial cash inflows to maintain ongoing operations, including funding for:

  • Ongoing inventory purchases
  • Accounts receivable financing
  • Equipment replacement and modernization
  • Seasonal operational cash swings
  • General working capital requirements
  • Technology platform updates
  • Facility and asset repairs
  • Long-term growth initiatives

For example, imagine two target businesses that each report $600,000 in adjusted annual earnings. The first enterprise requires minimal ongoing capital expenditure to sustain its daily footprint. The second enterprise consistently demands $200,000 per year in machinery upgrades and expanded inventory deposits simply to preserve its existing revenue base. These two opportunities represent vastly different underlying investments. Buyers must determine: After funding all necessary operational and capital requirements, how much net cash remains?

Exercise Healthy Skepticism Regarding Normalized Earnings Add-Backs

Financial presentations for private business sales almost always include normalizing adjustments and add-backs. Many of these adjustments are entirely legitimate. Sellers frequently remove expenses that were strictly personal, non-operational, highly unusual, or guaranteed not to recur post-closing.

However, an operational expense does not disappear from financial reality simply because it carries the label of an add-back. Buyers should rigorously question each proposed adjustment:

  • What specific underlying transaction is being added back to income?
  • Can the expense be independently verified with receipts or accounting records?
  • Has the underlying expenditure truly ceased, or will it persist after closing?
  • Does the exact same "one-time" expense recur across multiple past tax years?
  • Will operating the company require paying a third party to replace that service?
  • Is the proposed replacement salary adjustment for owner compensation grounded in realistic market rates?

A seller may feel fully justified in recasting historical financial metrics. The buyer's responsibility is to verify whether those adjusted figures accurately reflect your future cash flows.

Customer Concentration Significantly Alters Deal Risk

A firm supported by hundreds of recurring clients presents a fundamentally different risk profile than an entity reliant on a handful of major accounts. Consider two hypothetical businesses that each generate $2 million in annual revenue. Company A's largest single customer accounts for 4% of total sales. Company B's largest single customer generates 40% of overall sales volume.

Even if their income statements appear identical in terms of net margins, Company B carries substantial structural risk. Prior to submitting a formal offer, buyers must carefully evaluate:

  • The firm's top customer accounts by volume
  • The exact percentage of total revenue tied to each major customer
  • The tenure and history of those primary client relationships
  • Specific underlying contract terms and conditions
  • Upcoming contract expiration and renewal dates
  • Historical client retention and churn rates
  • Whether key relationships are tied to the firm's brand or personally to the selling owner

This identical level of scrutiny must extend to key product suppliers, primary referral channels, and exclusive distribution networks. High customer or vendor concentration does not automatically make a transaction unviable, but you should know you're buying that risk so it can be appropriately factored into purchase price and deal terms.

Thoroughly Analyze Balance Sheet Quality

While the income statement provides insight into operating performance, the balance sheet frequently reveals where hidden liabilities and asset quality risks reside. When evaluating a prospective acquisition target, closely review the following balance sheet accounts:

• Accounts receivable aged schedules
  • Accounts payable balances
  • Physical inventory valuations
  • Accrued operational liabilities
  • Short- and long-term debt instruments
  • Customer advance deposits
  • Deferred revenue obligations
  • Outstanding loans to or from owners
  • Net working capital balances

For instance, an asset schedule displaying $500,000 in total accounts receivable appears to represent substantial value. However, if detailed aging reports reveal that $150,000 of those balances have been delinquent for more than six months, their true collectible value is questionable. Similarly, inventory balances may be overstated if the stock includes obsolete goods or slow-moving items that cannot be sold at book value. Furthermore, a firm showing consistent profits may suffer from deferred capital maintenance, requiring immediate post-closing expenditures to replace aging equipment. Identifying these items before entering binding negotiations is essential to accurately projecting post-acquisition cash flow.

Working Capital Targets Directly Affect Net Proceeds at Closing

Most commercial acquisition contracts establish a specific target level of net working capital that must remain inside the enterprise at the time of closing. This contractual mechanism converts balance sheet quality directly into purchase price dollars. If outstanding receivables prove uncollectible, inventory valuations are adjusted downward, or unrecorded liabilities emerge, the resulting net working capital adjustment can alter the final cash required at closing. Understanding how working capital is defined, measured, and calculated is vital before assuming balance sheet assets will transfer at face value.

Cash-Basis Financial Accounting Requires Accrual Conversion

A significant percentage of small and mid-sized private companies maintain their accounting records on a cash basis. To evaluate true operating performance, an acquisition buyer must frequently restate those figures onto an accrual basis.

Converting cash-basis records to accrual accounting often uncovers earned revenues that remain uncollected in accounts receivable, incurred operating bills that remain unpaid in accounts payable, customer deposits collected for work not yet performed, accrued payroll liabilities, or other binding commitments not reflected on cash receipts ledgers. While cash-basis accounting may serve the seller's simple daily tracking or tax reporting, your acquisition analysis may require a different view of the economics than the seller normally uses to run or report the business.

Consider the Value of a Quality of Earnings Review on Larger Transactions

When evaluating larger or more complex acquisition opportunities, buyers often engage an independent accounting firm to perform a formal Quality of Earnings (QoE) review. A QoE report goes beyond a standard financial statement audit. It is a targeted transaction advisory engagement designed to analyze normalized EBITDA, identify quality of revenue, evaluate historical add-backs, model working capital requirements, and uncover potential risks affecting sustainable earnings performance.

While smaller transactions may not warrant a full third-party QoE engagement, the core principle remains vital across all deal sizes: Do not rely solely on the earnings number you were handed. Understand how it was built.

Tax Transaction Structure Directly Dictates Deal Value

Determining the tax structure of an acquisition is a strategic task that buyers should address before signing a definitive purchase agreement or letter of intent. Acquiring the assets of an enterprise versus purchasing the legal equity/stock of the entity yields vastly different tax outcomes for both buyer and seller.

In a standard taxable asset acquisition, the overall purchase price is allocated across the specific tangible and intangible assets acquired. This allocation establishes the buyer's initial tax basis in those assets, directly determining future tax depreciation and amortization deductions. Under federal tax rules, acquired intangible assets—including commercial goodwill—are generally amortized on a straight-line basis over a 15-year period. When applicable, both buyer and seller report this agreed purchase price allocation to the IRS using Form 8594, binding both parties to consistent tax reporting.

By contrast, an equity or stock acquisition functions differently. The buyer establishes a tax basis in the acquired corporate stock or ownership units, while the underlying tax basis of the company's internal assets generally remains unchanged unless a specific tax election or specialized transaction structure applies. This fundamental structural distinction directly impacts future tax deductions and long-term investment yields, explaining why buyers and sellers frequently hold opposing preferences regarding deal structure. Do not wait until after the purchase agreement is signed to begin asking about the tax consequences. While legal counsel drafts the transaction agreements, your tax professional should evaluate how the proposed deal structure impacts your net cash flow and tax liabilities.

Asset Purchases Do Not Automatically Eliminate State Successor Tax Liabilities

Buyers frequently assume that structuring a transaction as an asset purchase completely insulates them from the seller's historical business liabilities. Relying blindly on this assumption can lead to unexpected tax assessments.

State tax statutes vary considerably across jurisdictions, but many states enforce successor-liability, bulk-sale, withholding, or tax-clearance rules. Under these provisions, a buyer can be held liable for unpaid state sales, use, or employment taxes owed by the seller if mandatory notification, tax clearance, or escrow withholding procedures are omitted. Because these requirements differ by state and tax type, buyers must confirm prior to closing whether specific state tax clearances or withholding procedures apply. This is exactly the kind of issue that is much easier to address before the money changes hands.

Incorporate Acquisition Debt Financing Into Your Cash Flow Analysis

An enterprise that appears financially viable on an unlevered basis can quickly become cash-constrained once acquisition debt service is introduced. Financial projections must model net cash flows after accounting for mandatory debt service payments.

Buyers should evaluate whether post-debt cash flows are sufficient to:

  • Provide adequate owner compensation
  • Maintain appropriate net working capital levels
  • Fund recurring equipment replacement and maintenance
  • Withstand an unexpected revenue downturn or soft quarter
  • Reinvest in long-term operational growth
  • Service ongoing acquisition loan payments with an adequate margin of safety

If Small Business Administration (SBA) loan programs are central to your acquisition financing strategy, verify current underwriting rules and guidelines with an active SBA lender early in the process. Relying on financing parameters from past years can lead to false assumptions, as SBA rules surrounding borrower eligibility, buyer equity injections, and debt seller notes evolve over time. In fact, business brokers surveyed by BizBuySell frequently cite changing SBA lending criteria as a key source of friction in closing transactions.

Retain Adequate Working Capital for Post-Closing Operations

A common mistake among first-time buyers is underestimating post-closing cash needs: How much cash will you need the day after closing? Exhausting all available liquid capital simply to pay the initial acquisition purchase price leaves the business exposed to operational disruption.

Beyond the baseline purchase price, new owners require immediate post-closing liquidity to fund:

  • Initial payroll cycles
  • Target inventory purchases
  • Day-to-day working capital needs
  • Commercial insurance premiums
  • Technology platform updates and licenses
  • Marketing and customer acquisition campaigns
  • Targeted employee recruitment
  • Immediate equipment repairs or additions
  • Closing legal and accounting fees
  • Unplanned customer churn or unexpected repairs

Even a fundamentally sound business can experience severe operational strain if a buyer completes the transaction without sufficient cash reserves. Calculate the precise capital required to purchase the business, then calculate the capital required to successfully own and operate the business.

Obtain an Independent Financial Review Before Committing to Terms

The process of acquiring a business is inherently exciting. That excitement makes an objective, independent financial evaluation indispensable. Once a buyer begins visualizing themselves running the business, it becomes easy to overlook warning signs that warrant closer examination.

An experienced tax and accounting professional provides an objective review of key deal elements, including:

  • Verifying whether historical reported earnings are supported by underlying records
  • Determining whether SDE or EBITDA represents the appropriate evaluation metric
  • Analyzing proposed seller add-backs for economic validity
  • Calculating the true cost to hire replacement management for owner duties
  • Determining the actual working capital required to sustain operations
  • Evaluating the quality and collectibility of accounts receivable and inventory
  • Projecting realistic post-closing cash flows after debt service
  • Analyzing how the proposed asset vs. equity structure impacts long-term tax yields
  • Identifying required state tax clearances and successor liability risks

The objective of an independent review is not to decide whether you should buy the company, but to ensure you fully comprehend what the financial data reveals before executing a binding agreement.

Structured Business Acquisitions Offer Immense Potential When Properly Evaluated

Acquiring an established business provides prospective business owners with significant operational advantages that a startup cannot replicate from day one: existing clients, trained staff, proven operational systems, established top-line revenue, and immediate cash flow potential.

However, acquiring an ongoing entity also means taking on its financial history, capital requirements, customer concentration risks, and potential tax obligations depending on how the deal is executed. The ultimate goal is not to search for a flawless business, but to understand the target's underlying financial mechanics well enough to negotiate a price and structure that reflects its true value to you.

title: Accountable Plans: Maximizing Tax-Free Employee Reimbursements
excerpt: Discover how setting up an accountable plan allows businesses to reimburse employee expenses tax-free while maintaining IRS compliance and payroll accuracy.
description: Learn how an accountable plan keeps employee reimbursements tax-free, ensures IRS compliance, and protects business deductions.

blocks.html:
An accountable plan offers one of the most effective methods for a business to reimburse employees for legitimate business expenses without converting those payments into taxable compensation. When structured and executed properly, your business can cover ordinary and necessary costs tax-free, enabling employees to avoid income and payroll taxes on their reimbursements while the business maintains its tax deduction for the underlying expense.

For business owners, an accountable plan serves as an essential compliance tool that supports cash flow. For employees, it ensures they are fully repaid for out-of-pocket workplace expenses without facing unintended income tax liabilities. However, the IRS rules governing these arrangements are strict, and informal reimbursement practices frequently fail to meet required standards.

Understanding the Fundamentals of an Accountable Plan

To qualify as an accountable plan under IRS guidelines, a reimbursement arrangement must satisfy three foundational criteria:

  1. A clear business connection: Expenses must be incurred in connection with performing services as an employee.

  2. Substantiation: Employees must adequately substantiate expenses within a reasonable timeframe.

  3. Return of excess funds: Employees must return any excess advances or reimbursements within a reasonable period.

When an arrangement meets all three conditions, reimbursements are excluded from employee gross income, do not require reporting on Form W-2, and are exempt from federal income tax withholding and FICA taxes. Conversely, if an arrangement fails any of these core requirements, reimbursements are treated as taxable wages subject to standard employment taxes and withholding rules.

Key Advantages for Business Owners

Implementing a formal accountable plan delivers concrete financial and administrative benefits to an organization:

  • Keeps payroll records clean by separating official expense reimbursements from standard compensation.

  • Mitigates the operational risk of the IRS reclassifying expense reimbursements as taxable wages.

  • Establishes a robust, defensible paper trail for tax-deductible business expenses.

  • Streamlines accounting overhead when per diem reimbursement methods are utilized.

For S corporations and closely held companies, accurate reimbursement classification is particularly vital. It prevents artificial wage inflation while giving business owners a clear mechanism to cover necessary operating costs.

Scope of Coverable Business Expenses

Accountable plans generally encompass a wide array of ordinary and necessary expenses, including business travel, vehicle mileage, lodging, meals, and workplace supplies. Reimbursements for overnight travel away from home remain tax-exempt for employees specifically when issued under a qualified accountable plan.

Transportation costs follow these identical criteria, requiring thorough employee substantiation before any tax-free reimbursement can occur.

Documentation and Recordkeeping Requirements

Inadequate documentation is one of the most common reasons reimbursement plans fail compliance checks. Vague expense descriptions like "travel" or "miscellaneous business exp" fall short of IRS expectations. Employees must detail the exact business purpose behind every transaction.

At minimum, expense records must document:

  • Date of the expense,

  • Time (when applicable),

  • Location or place,

  • Dollar amount, and

  • Specific business purpose.

Employees must back up these details with supporting documentary evidence such as detailed receipts, bills, or canceled checks. Employers typically require original receipts or legible copies, and employees should retain duplicate copies for their personal records.

Evaluating Receipt Requirements

As a general rule, detailed receipts are mandatory to satisfy substantiation requirements, except when reimbursements are calculated using approved per diem rates. Utilizing per diem methods can significantly simplify recordkeeping for qualifying travel expenses.

Special Considerations for Business Meals

Meal reimbursements are subject to strict accountable plan standards. While traveling away from home follows set rules, non-travel business meals—such as client meetings or overtime meals—must be substantiated using the actual expense method rather than estimated amounts.

Adhering to Mandatory Timing Rules

Timing is a critical component of accountable plan compliance. Both expense substantiation and the return of unspent advances must occur within a defined, reasonable timeframe. Excessive delays in submitting expense documentation or returning surplus advances can invalidate an otherwise compliant plan.

IRS Safe Harbor Timelines Explained

The IRS provides specific safe harbor methods to help businesses determine what constitutes a "reasonable period of time":

  • The Fixed-Date Method: Establishes explicit calendar benchmarks to preserve tax-free status:

    • 60 Days for Substantiation: Employees must submit expense reports with receipts and business details within 60 days of paying or incurring the cost (or within 60 days of returning from a business trip).

    • 30 Days for Advances: Cash advances must be distributed no earlier than 30 days before the employee anticipates incurring the business cost.

    • 120 Days to Return Excess: Any unspent advance or excess per diem money must be returned within 120 days of the expense date.

  • The Periodic-Statement Standard: Employers issue a quarterly expense statement to employees, giving them 120 days from the statement date to substantiate expenses or return excess advances.

  • Company Discretion: Businesses are free to set tighter internal deadlines (such as a 30-day submission rule) to keep accounting current. However, extending submission windows beyond the 60-day safe harbor risks audit adjustments unless unique facts and circumstances justify the delay.

Consequences of Missing Compliance Deadlines

If an employee fails to substantiate an expense within the required timeframe, the reimbursement arrangement legally converts into a non-accountable plan for that transaction. Consequently, the employer must treat the payment as taxable wages, report it on Form W-2, and withhold required payroll and income taxes.

Handling Surplus Advances and Excess Reimbursements

Returning excess reimbursements within a reasonable window is an indispensable element of an accountable plan. If an employee retains surplus funds beyond the permitted timeline, the plan's tax-favored status breaks down, turning tax-free payouts into taxable wages.

Developing an Effective Expense Reimbursement Form

The IRS does not mandate a specific standardized reimbursement template. However, to ensure full compliance, a company's expense report form should collect comprehensive detail, including:

  • Employee name,

  • Date of request,

  • Dates of travel or expense,

  • Vendor or merchant name,

  • Business purpose,

  • Amount incurred,

  • Attached receipt verification,

  • Detailed mileage logs (if applicable),

  • Prior advance amounts received,

  • Net reimbursement requested, and

  • Amount to be returned if an advance exceeded actual costs.

Sample Accountable Plan Policy Statement

Organizations can adapt the following policy language for internal employee handbooks or operations manuals:

Accountable Plan Policy
The company will reimburse employees for ordinary and necessary business expenses incurred on behalf of the company, provided the expenses have a business connection, are properly substantiated, and any excess advances or reimbursements are returned within a reasonable period of time. Employees must submit expense reports with sufficient detail to identify the amount, date, place, and business purpose of each expense, together with receipts or other supporting documentation when required. Reimbursements made under this policy are intended to qualify as reimbursements under an accountable plan and are not intended to be treated as wages. Any amount advanced in excess of substantiated business expenses must be returned promptly.

Common Operational Challenges to Avoid

Several recurring operational missteps can jeopardize an accountable plan:

  • Vague Descriptions: Broad labels like "client lunch" lack required context; reports should specify who attended and the business reason.

  • Missing Receipts: Unsubstantiated items requiring documentation may be denied or converted to taxable income.

  • Late Submissions: Delayed expense reports make it difficult to satisfy IRS reasonable-time rules.

  • Unreconciled Advances: Failing to systematically reconcile advances against actual receipts undermines plan compliance.

  • Meal & Entertainment Confusion: Misapplying rules governing travel meals versus non-travel business meetings.

  • Owner & Related-Party Transactions: Transactions involving owner-employees receive heightened IRS scrutiny, especially regarding travel and per diem rates.

Best Practices for Maintaining Compliance

To protect your plan's accountable status, incorporate these core operational habits:

  • Maintain a formal written policy,

  • Enforce a predictable, regular expense submission schedule,

  • Require detailed receipts wherever applicable,

  • Clearly define standards for establishing business purpose,

  • Reconcile cash advances promptly to recover unspent funds,

  • Apply per diem methods strictly within regulatory guidelines, and

  • Keep reimbursement accounting strictly separated from payroll records.

Optimizing Your Expense Reimbursement Strategy

An accountable plan offers an ideal win-win scenario: employees receive tax-free reimbursement for legitimate business expenses while the company maintains clean payroll accounting and preserves its tax deductions. Maintaining these benefits simply requires strict adherence to business connection, detailed substantiation, and prompt return of excess funds.

If you need guidance establishing or auditing an accountable plan for your business, contact our office today to schedule a consultation.

title: Why Clean Financial Statements Matter When You Sell a Business
excerpt: Discover why clean, consistent financial statements and trusted accounting guidance build buyer confidence, streamline due diligence, and maximize value when selling a business.
description: Clean, consistent financial statements can help buyers understand your business, support due diligence, and build confidence in the numbers.

blocks.html:
A business owner may spend years building a strong company and still discover something frustrating when it comes time to sell:

The buyer cannot see the business the way the owner does.

You know why margins changed. You know why one quarter was unusually strong. You know which customer paid late, why inventory increased, or why payroll jumped.

The buyer does not have that history in their head.

They have the financial statements.

And if those statements are inconsistent, outdated, unreconciled, or difficult to explain, the buyer has to spend more time figuring out what the business is actually doing.

That is why clean financial statements matter.

But there is another piece that matters just as much:

Who can explain those financial statements when the questions begin?

A buyer may be more comfortable when the numbers are not only clean, but when there is a tax or accounting professional who understands how they were prepared, knows the history, and can explain what changed and why.

Clean Does Not Mean "Made to Look Better"

Clean financial statements are not statements designed to make a business appear more profitable than it really is.

They are statements that are:

  • Current

  • Reconciled

  • Prepared consistently

  • Properly classified

  • Supported by documentation

  • Easy to explain

The goal is not to dress up the business.

The goal is to make the financial picture accurate and understandable.

A buyer is not just evaluating whether the numbers look good.

They are trying to decide whether the numbers are reliable.

Consistency Builds Confidence

A buyer may review several years of financial information.

They want to understand patterns.

Is revenue growing?

Are margins stable?

Are payroll costs increasing faster than sales?

Are receivables getting older?

Is the business carrying more debt?

Those questions are easier to answer when the financial statements have been prepared consistently from period to period.

That is where having a disciplined financial-reporting process begins to matter.

If accounts are classified differently every year, financial statements are closed months late, or large adjustments are made only at tax time, it becomes harder to determine whether a change in the numbers reflects the business or the reporting.

A consistent process reduces that uncertainty.

A Reliable Monthly Close Matters

One of the clearest signs of strong financial reporting is a regular monthly close.

That means the books are not simply updated once a year before the tax return is prepared.

Bank accounts are reconciled. Receivables and payables are reviewed. Balance-sheet accounts are examined. Significant transactions are recorded consistently. Financial statements are produced on a predictable schedule.

Over time, that creates something valuable:

A history of financial information prepared the same way, month after month.

That can make a future buyer more comfortable than financial statements that had to be reconstructed immediately before a sale.

It also gives the owner better information while they are still running the business.

Cash-Basis Financials Can Create Surprises

Many privately held businesses maintain some or all of their financial records on a cash basis.

That may work well for tax or day-to-day purposes, depending on the business and applicable tax rules.

But buyers and transaction advisors may want to understand the company on an accrual basis.

That difference can matter.

Under cash-basis accounting, revenue and expenses generally appear when cash changes hands.

Under accrual accounting, revenue and expenses are generally recognized when they are earned or incurred.

The distinction can change how the business looks.

For example:

  • A company may have completed significant work but not yet collected payment.

  • Expenses may have been incurred but not yet paid.

  • Customer deposits may have been received for work that still needs to be performed.

  • Accounts receivable and accounts payable may materially affect working capital.

When someone converts the business from cash to accrual for transaction analysis, reported earnings and working capital can change.

That can surprise an owner who has spent years looking primarily at cash-basis reports.

This is one reason to involve a tax or accounting professional early. The owner can begin understanding what the business may look like through the reporting framework a buyer is likely to use.

The Balance Sheet Can Tell a Different Story

Owners naturally focus on the profit-and-loss statement.

Buyers often look just as closely at the balance sheet.

They may want to understand:

  • Accounts receivable

  • Accounts payable

  • Inventory

  • Debt

  • Accrued expenses

  • Owner or shareholder loans

  • Cash

  • Working capital

  • Fixed assets

A business may report strong profits while carrying old receivables, questionable inventory, unexplained liabilities, or accounts that have not been reconciled in years.

Those items can create questions even when the income statement looks strong.

Old Receivables Can Become a Deal Issue

Accounts receivable are a good example.

An owner may look at the total balance and see money customers owe the business.

A buyer may ask a different question:

How much of this is actually collectible?

If a meaningful portion of the balance is 90, 120, or 180 days old, the buyer may question whether the receivable balance is worth what the financial statements suggest.

That can matter because many transactions establish a target level of working capital that the business is expected to deliver at closing.

If receivables turn out to be overstated or uncollectible, that issue may come back to the seller.

That is why aging schedules, reconciliations, and ongoing review matter long before a transaction begins.

Inventory Deserves the Same Attention

Inventory-heavy businesses can face similar questions.

Is the inventory count accurate?

Is some of it obsolete?

Has slow-moving inventory accumulated?

Are costing methods being applied consistently?

Does the balance on the financial statements match what is actually on hand?

Again, the issue is not whether inventory is high or low.

The question is whether the buyer can understand and trust the number.

Financial-Reporting Policies Should Be Consistent

Sometimes the problem is not the dollar amount.

It is how transactions have been treated.

For example, similar expenses may be classified differently from year to year. Similar repairs may be treated differently from one period to another. Certain costs may move between cost of goods sold and operating expenses.

There may be legitimate reasons for some differences.

But inconsistent treatment makes it harder to compare performance over time.

A buyer trying to understand gross margin, operating expenses, or normalized earnings may have difficulty determining whether a trend is real or simply the result of changes in reporting treatment.

Consistency helps make those comparisons more meaningful.

The Person Who Can Explain the Numbers Matters

This may be one of the most overlooked parts of preparing for a sale.

During due diligence, buyers ask questions.

Sometimes a lot of them.

Why did this account increase three years ago?

What caused margins to fall in this period?

Why does this balance differ from the prior year?

What is included in this expense category?

Why did receivables spike?

If a tax or accounting professional has been involved consistently and understands the history, those questions may be answered quickly.

If nobody knows the answer, the owner may have to search through years of transactions, emails, bank records, and old files trying to reconstruct what happened.

The difference is not just convenience.

It can affect confidence.

When a buyer asks a financial question and receives a clear, documented explanation, the process feels more controlled.

When every question creates a new investigation, uncertainty grows.

Clean Financials Make Other Transaction Questions Easier

Issues such as add-backs, tax-return differences, lender underwriting, and the level of assurance provided by financial statements may all arise during a sale.

But clean, consistent financial reporting makes all of those conversations easier.

If the underlying records are current, reconciled, and well supported, there is a stronger foundation for answering whatever questions come next.

That is why financial cleanup should not begin after a letter of intent is signed.

It should begin before anyone is under pressure.

Think Ahead About the Level of Financial Reporting

Depending on the size and type of transaction, a buyer or lender may ask for a particular level of financial reporting.

Some financial statements are compiled, reviewed, or audited. Compiled statements provide no assurance, reviewed statements provide limited assurance, and audited statements provide reasonable assurance.

Many privately held businesses never need reviewed or audited statements. But if a future buyer or lender may ask for them, it helps to know early. Reviews and audits are performed by an independent CPA firm under professional standards, and that work goes much more smoothly when the books are already current, reconciled, and well documented.

It is also common for businesses to work with one advisor on day-to-day bookkeeping, tax, and financial reporting and to engage a separate firm when a review or audit is needed. In fact, professional independence rules can limit whether the same firm provides both types of services.

Either way, the groundwork is the same. The cleaner and more consistent your records are, the easier any level of financial reporting becomes.

Do not wait until the transaction is underway to decide what level of financial reporting you may need.

Give Yourself Time to Build a Track Record

Some financial issues can be cleaned up quickly.

Others cannot.

A buyer may want to see several periods of consistent reporting.

They may want to know whether margins are stable, whether receivables are improving, or whether inventory is being managed properly.

One clean quarter may not answer those questions.

With enough lead time, you can:

  • Reconcile old accounts

  • Review stale receivables

  • Clean up inventory records

  • Standardize classifications

  • Document owner loans

  • Establish a monthly close

  • Begin preparing accrual-basis financial statements, if appropriate

  • Clear outdated balance-sheet items

  • Build a history of timely, consistent financial statements

That history can be difficult to create at the last minute.

We Can Help You See What a Buyer Will See

If selling the business may be in your future, one useful exercise is to look at the financial statements as though you had never seen the company before.

Would the numbers make sense?

Would the trends be clear?

Would balance-sheet accounts hold up to scrutiny?

Would cash-basis reporting create surprises when viewed on an accrual basis?

Are the financial statements closed consistently every month?

If a buyer asked what changed three years ago, could someone answer the question?

Those are the kinds of issues we can help you evaluate before a buyer starts asking.

Clean Financial Statements Create More Than Order

Clean financial statements do more than make due diligence easier.

They can help create confidence.

They make it easier to understand earnings, working capital, trends, and risk.

And when there is a tax or accounting professional who understands the business and can explain the history, questions can be answered with documentation rather than reconstruction.

The buyer will still perform their own diligence.

But a clearer financial history can make that process more efficient and reduce avoidable uncertainty.

If selling your business may be part of your future, talk with our firm before the process begins.

We can help you evaluate your reporting, improve consistency, identify areas that may create questions, and begin preparing the financial statements for the scrutiny that comes with a sale.

Thinking about selling your business someday? Contact our firm and start strengthening your financial reporting now.

title: Crowdfunding and Taxes: What Organizers and Contributors Need to Know
excerpt: A comprehensive guide explaining the tax implications of donation-based, rewards-based, and equity crowdfunding for both campaign organizers and backers.
description: Crowdfunding can have unexpected tax consequences. Learn how personal donations, rewards, investments, Form 1099-K, and gift tax rules may apply.

blocks.html:
Crowdfunding has opened the door for people to raise money for almost anything: medical bills, family emergencies, creative projects, business startups, and even investment opportunities. But the tax rules depend heavily on why the money was raised, what the contributor received in return, and how the platform processed the payment. For taxpayers, the key lesson is simple: crowdfunding is not automatically a tax-free “gift,” and it is not automatically taxable income either. The tax result depends on the facts and circumstances.

If you are involved in a crowdfunding campaign as either the organizer or the contributor, the three most common categories to understand are:

  • Donation-based campaigns

  • Rewards-based campaigns

  • Equity-based campaigns

Each one creates different tax consequences.

Donation-Based Crowdfunding: Personal Causes vs. Charitable Causes

Donation-based crowdfunding is often used for personal needs such as medical bills, funeral expenses, disaster recovery, or living expenses. It is also used for charitable fundraising. These two situations may look similar online, but they are treated very differently for tax purposes.

  • Personal Donation Campaigns - If a crowdfunding campaign is set up for an individual’s personal hardship and the contributor gives money without expecting anything meaningful in return, the payment received may qualify as a gift rather than taxable income. Under the gift standard, the payment must come from “detached and disinterested generosity” and not be made in exchange for goods, services, or other economic benefit. In practice, campaigns raised to help with medical bills are often treated as nontaxable gifts when the facts fit that standard.

    o    Organizer: For the organizer, this means the funds may not be taxable if they truly qualify as gifts. But the organizer should not assume that a crowdfunding page label like “donation” automatically controls the tax result. The IRS looks at the actual facts, including whether the contributor expected something of value in return.

    o    Contributor: For the contributor, a personal gift to another individual is generally not deductible as a charitable contribution. That is an important point: even if the payment feels charitable or compassionate, it usually does not qualify for a tax deduction unless it was made to a qualified charity.

  • Charitable Donation Campaigns - A different result applies when the crowdfunding campaign is run by a qualified section 501(c)(3) charitable organization. In that situation, the donor may be able to claim a charitable contribution deduction if all normal charitable rules are satisfied including an IRS qualified donation receipt. But if the donor receives goods or services in return, part or all of the payment may be nondeductible.

    For example, if a donor gives $100 to a charity crowdfunding campaign and receives a shirt worth $25, only the amount above the fair market value of the shirt may be deductible, assuming all other requirements are met. The fair market value of any goods or services given back to the donor should be determined in advance and disclosed.

    For the organizer, the charitable status matters a great deal. Contributions to a private individual are not charitable gifts to a qualified charity, even if the campaign is framed as “helping out”. For the contributor, the deduction depends on whether the recipient is a qualified charity and whether the donor received anything of value in return.

Rewards-Based Crowdfunding: Usually Taxable to the Organizer

Rewards-based crowdfunding is the model used by platforms like Kickstarter and Indiegogo. Contributors give money in exchange for a product, service, or other reward. The reward might be a T-shirt, coffee mug, event ticket, digital content, or early access to a product.

This type of campaign is usually much more like a sale than a gift. If the contributor receives a reward with real value, the payment generally is not a gift because there is a quid pro quo.

  • Organizer Tax Treatment - For the organizer, rewards-based crowdfunding is often taxable income. The money received is generally included in gross income unless the organizer can show that some exclusion applies. If the campaign supports a business or trade, the organizer will usually report the proceeds as business income.

    The organizer may generally deduct ordinary and necessary expenses connected to the campaign if the activity is carried on with a profit motive and qualifies as a trade or business. Those expenses can include:

    o   platform fees

    o   production costs for the rewards

    o   marketing costs

    o   other ordinary business expenses.

    If the crowdfunding effort is not a for-profit activity, deductions may be limited or unavailable under the business rules. In other words, an organizer should not assume that every cost is deductible simply because the campaign was expensive to run.

  • Contributor Tax Treatment - For the contributor, the tax issue is usually not deduction-based. Instead, the question is whether the payment is a purchase, a donation, or something else. If the contributor gets merchandise or another tangible benefit, the payment is generally treated as consideration for what was received, not as a deductible charitable gift.

    If the backer receives only a token item of insubstantial value, the facts may still support gift treatment in some situations. But taxpayers should be careful here: many crowdfunding rewards are more than token items, and the presence of a real reward generally weakens any gift argument.

Equity-Based Crowdfunding: An Investment, Not a Gift

Equity crowdfunding is different from donation-based or rewards-based campaigns because the contributor receives an ownership interest, such as stock or a partnership interest, in exchange for the contribution.

• Organizer Tax Treatment - For the organizer, money received in exchange for an equity interest is generally a capital contribution, not taxable income at receipt. The organizer is bringing in investors rather than customers or donors. That means the campaign is being treated like a real investment transaction, not a gift or sale of merchandise.

    However, this also means the organizer must treat the arrangement as an actual securities offering with related reporting and compliance obligations. The SEC crowdfunding rules require use of a registered intermediary, disclosure filings, annual reporting, and other investor protection requirements. That is not a small issue. A business that takes equity crowdfunding seriously must also take its compliance obligations seriously.

  • Contributor Tax Treatment - For the contributor, equity crowdfunding is not a charitable contribution. It is an investment. The contributor’s tax basis in the investment is generally the amount contributed. That basis matters later if the investor sells the interest or receives distributions.

    Contributors should also understand that investment returns may create future taxable income in the form of dividends, capital gains, or other taxable proceeds depending on the facts. In other words, equity crowdfunding may offer growth potential, but it also creates the same tax issues that come with any investment.

  • A Quick Note on SEC Crowdfunding Rules - If a crowdfunding campaign is offering investors an ownership interest, it may fall under SEC crowdfunding rules. Under these rules, a business can generally raise up to $5 million in a 12-month period through a registered online intermediary.

    For investors, the amount they can put in depends on income and net worth. If either their income or net worth is less than $124,000, they can invest the greater of $2,500 or 5% of the higher of their income or net worth. If both their income and net worth are $124,000 or more, they can invest up to 10% of the higher of their income or net worth, with a maximum of $124,000 in a 12-month period.

The 1099-K Issue: Just Because You Receive the Form Doesn’t Mean It’s Taxable

A common source of confusion is the Form 1099-K. Crowdfunding platforms and payment processors may issue 1099-K forms when the reporting thresholds are met. For 2025 and later reporting years, the general federal third-party settlement threshold is more than $20,000 and more than 200 transactions.

This is important because taxpayers sometimes assume a 1099-K automatically means the entire amount is taxable income. It does not. A form 1099-K is an information reporting document, not a final tax determination. If a taxpayer receives one in error or for a nontaxable campaign, the taxpayer should still report the return appropriately and keep records supporting the correct tax treatment.

For organizers, this means good recordkeeping is essential. Track who contributed, how much was received, whether anything was given back, and how the funds were used. For contributors, it means keeping records of what you gave, whether you received anything in return, and whether the recipient was a qualified charity and provided a mandated IRS donation receipt.

Gift Tax Considerations Can Apply Too

Even when a crowdfunding payment qualifies as a gift for income tax purposes, the gift tax rules may still matter. If a person makes a gift above the annual exclusion amount to one recipient, a gift tax return may be required. The annual exclusion for 2026 is $19,000 per donee.

That does not mean tax is always owed when the exclusion is exceeded. It means the donor may need to file a Form 709, which is the donor’s responsibility, not the recipient’s. This is especially important in larger family or personal support campaigns where one person contributes a substantial amount to another individual.

Practical Takeaways

Here is the simplest way to think about crowdfunding tax treatment:

  • Personal Donation Campaigns may be treated as gifts if the donor does not receive anything in return, but they are not tax-deductible charitable contributions unless the payment is made to a qualified charity.

  • Charitable Crowdfunding can be deductible, but only if the organization is a qualified section 501(c)(3) charity and the donor meets the normal substantiation rules and an IRS qualified donation receipt is provided.

  • Rewards-Based Campaigns are usually taxable to the organizer because they are more like sales than gifts.

  • Equity-Based Campaigns are generally capital contributions to the organizer and investments for the contributor.

  • Form 1099-K reporting does not decide whether the money is taxable; the underlying facts control.

Final Thoughts

Crowdfunding can be a powerful way to raise money, but tax treatment depends on substance, not labels. It may seem simple on the surface, but the tax rules can quickly become complicated depending on how the campaign is structured and what the contributor receives in return. If you are involved in a crowdfunding campaign and want to understand the tax consequences, this office can help with guidance tailored to your situation so you can avoid surprises and move forward with confidence.

title: Thinking About Selling Your Business? Start Preparing Your Financials Now
excerpt: Preparing to sell a business requires clean, credible financial records. Learn how early financial preparation, add-back documentation, and lender alignment impact deal value.
description: Planning to sell your business someday? Clean, credible financials can support buyer confidence, financing, and a smoother sale.

blocks.html:
A significant wave of business ownership transitions is underway.

Project Equity estimates that 2.9 million U.S. businesses are owned by people age 55 or older, representing about $6.5 trillion in annual revenue. As more longtime owners begin thinking about retirement and succession, an enormous number of privately held companies will change hands in the years ahead.

If your business may eventually be one of them, one lesson matters more than many owners realize:

Preparing to sell should begin long before the business goes on the market.

And one of the best places to start is with your financial records.

A buyer may love your company. They may understand the market, appreciate the customer base, and see growth opportunities you have not pursued yet.

But before they write a check, they are going to want to understand the numbers.

So will their lender. So will the professionals helping them evaluate the transaction.

That is why clean, credible financials can influence much more than whether due diligence goes smoothly. They can affect trust, financing, negotiations, deal terms, and ultimately the price a buyer is willing to support.

A Buyer Is Not Just Buying Your Story

Most business owners can explain their company better than anyone.

You know why one year was unusually strong. You know why margins dipped two years ago. You know which expenses were owner-related, which projects were unusual, and which costs are unlikely to continue under new ownership.

A buyer does not know any of that.

They see the records.

They may review several years of financial statements, tax returns, payroll records, bank activity, accounts receivable, debt, capital expenditures, customer concentration, owner compensation, and other operating information.

And they are trying to answer one central question:

Can I trust the financial story I am being told?

Consider two businesses that each report $1 million in annual earnings.

One owner can provide consistent financial statements, reconciled accounts, tax returns that support the numbers, and clear documentation for unusual expenses.

The other has unreconciled accounts, personal expenses mixed into the business, unsupported adjustments, and numbers that change depending on which report someone is reviewing.

The reported earnings may be identical.

The confidence level is not.

The Tax Strategy That Helped You May Look Different to a Buyer

This is where many owners encounter something they may not have considered.

For years, you may have worked with us to legitimately reduce taxable income through deductions, depreciation, compensation planning, timing strategies, or other appropriate tax-planning decisions.

Those strategies may have saved significant taxes.

But a buyer is looking at the business through a different lens.

They want to know how much the company can reliably earn in the future.

A seller may say:

“Once you account for owner-related and discretionary expenses, the business really earns more than the tax return suggests.”

The buyer or lender may respond:

“Can you support those adjustments?”

That does not mean the previous tax planning was wrong.

It means the strategies that made sense for tax planning may look different when someone is trying to establish the earnings and value of the company.

That is one reason to discuss a possible future sale with us early. Tax planning and exit planning do not exist in separate worlds.

This Is Where Add-Backs Enter the Conversation

If you sell your business, you are likely to hear the term add-back.

An add-back is generally an expense a seller argues should not reduce the ongoing earnings of the company because it is owner-specific, discretionary, unusual, or nonrecurring.

Examples might include certain owner expenses, family payroll, unusual consulting costs, one-time legal fees, or other expenses that may not continue after the transaction.

Some add-backs are relatively straightforward. Others receive much more scrutiny.

Suppose you tell a buyer that $150,000 of expenses should be added back to earnings. If those expenses are clearly documented and there is a reasonable explanation for why they will not continue, the buyer has something tangible to evaluate.

If someone has to reconstruct several years of transactions to figure out what actually happened, the same adjustment may be much harder to support.

The buyer is not simply paying for what you say the company earned.

They are deciding what they believe the company can continue to earn.

Uncertainty Can Become Part of the Deal

Sellers naturally focus on purchase price.

But uncertainty can affect far more than the headline number.

A buyer who is uncomfortable with the financial information may request more documentation, reduce valuation assumptions, hold back part of the purchase price, introduce an earnout, change working-capital requirements, or negotiate other protections into the transaction.

In other words, weak financial records are not merely a bookkeeping inconvenience.

They can become a negotiating issue.

Then the Lender Starts Asking Questions

Many business acquisitions involve financing.

That means the buyer may not be the only party evaluating your company's financial history.

A lender or underwriter may review historical earnings, cash flow, tax returns, existing debt, working-capital requirements, customer concentration, capital expenditures, and other financial information.

They want to understand whether the business can generate enough cash to support the debt used to acquire it.

If an underwriter cannot get comfortable with the numbers, the consequences can flow back to the seller.

The buyer may need more equity, different financing, a lower price, or a different transaction structure.

So financial credibility is not only about convincing the buyer.

It can also help the buyer get the transaction financed.

Your Tax Returns and Financial Statements Need to Tell a Coherent Story

Tax returns and financial statements serve different purposes, so differences between them can be completely legitimate.

But a buyer or lender may compare them.

They may want to understand why revenue, expenses, depreciation, owner compensation, inventory, or other items appear differently across the records.

The question is not whether every number matches perfectly.

It is whether the differences can be explained.

That becomes much easier when we have had time to understand the company's history and prepare before the sale process begins.

The Financial Statements Themselves May Matter

Not every financial statement provides the same level of assurance.

Compiled financial statements provide no assurance, reviewed financial statements provide limited assurance, and audited financial statements provide reasonable assurance.

That does not mean every business preparing for a sale needs reviewed or audited financial statements.

The appropriate level depends on the business, the transaction, and what a prospective buyer or lender may require.

If a sale is on your horizon, this is worth discussing before a transaction begins rather than after someone requests a particular level of financial reporting.

Some Sellers Choose to Look for Problems Before the Buyer Does

Once a deal becomes serious, a buyer may commission a quality of earnings analysis, commonly called a QoE.

A QoE is not the same as a financial statement audit.

A QoE generally focuses on transaction-related questions such as the sustainability of earnings, unusual adjustments, revenue quality, working capital, customer concentration, and other factors that may affect how the business is evaluated.

Some sellers choose to conduct a sell-side QoE or another pre-sale financial review before going to market.

The logic is simple:

Would you rather discover an issue yourself or have the buyer discover it during due diligence?

Finding something early gives you time to understand it, document it, and decide whether anything needs to change before negotiations begin.

Not every transaction needs a formal QoE.

But almost every seller can benefit from knowing what a buyer is likely to find before the buyer begins looking.

Time Is One of Your Biggest Advantages

If a buyer discovers a financial issue during due diligence, you may have only days to explain it.

If you discover the same issue one or two years before a sale, you may have time to do something about it.

You may be able to reconcile accounts, improve documentation, separate personal and business expenses, clean up old receivables, improve inventory records, document unusual transactions, or establish more consistent reporting.

Some issues can be fixed quickly.

Others need history.

If a buyer wants to see whether margins are stable, whether an expense is truly nonrecurring, or whether cash flow is improving, one cleaned-up quarter may not be enough.

That is why early preparation matters.

We Can Help You See the Business the Way a Buyer Will

Because we already understand your company's tax returns, financial statements, payroll, owner compensation, debt, and major transactions, we can help you begin looking at the business from the outside.

Questions worth asking include:

  • Are the books current and reconciled?

  • Do the tax returns and financial statements tell a coherent story?

  • Are there expenses that may eventually be treated as add-backs?

  • Can those adjustments be documented?

  • Are there trends a buyer or lender is likely to question?

  • Is the current level of financial reporting appropriate?

  • Would a pre-sale financial review or QoE make sense?

  • Are today's tax strategies consistent with your longer-term exit plans?

You do not need to be ready to sell tomorrow to start asking these questions.

In fact, that is the point.

The Best Time to Prepare Is Before You Need to Explain Anything

You may have spent 20, 30, or 40 years building your company.

When the time comes to sell it, you want the financial records to help tell that story — not undermine it.

A clean financial history can help buyers understand the business, help lenders evaluate the transaction, and help you answer questions with confidence.

It can also reduce the chance that avoidable uncertainty becomes part of the negotiation.

If selling your business may be somewhere in your future, talk with us now.

We can help you review your financial records, identify issues worth addressing, and begin preparing for the questions a future buyer, lender, or advisor is likely to ask.

Thinking about selling your business someday? Contact our firm and start preparing before the sale process begins.

title: How QuickBooks and Meta's Muse Are Changing Small Business Accounting
excerpt: QuickBooks is joining Meta's Muse for Small Business. Discover how this AI integration impacts your bookkeeping, invoicing, and need for accurate financials.
description: QuickBooks is integrating with Meta's new AI platform, Muse for Small Business. Learn how this changes financial management and why accurate books still matter.

blocks.html:
QuickBooks users now have a new way to interact with their financial data—and it might not even require opening the QuickBooks app.

On October 1, Intuit announced that QuickBooks is officially joining Muse for Small Business, Meta's new AI-powered platform. This integration lets eligible businesses link their QuickBooks accounts to Muse, using conversational AI to handle specific financial tasks like drafting invoices, collecting payments, and pulling business insights.

It points to a clear shift in the accounting software landscape: platforms are moving beyond simply recording data, relying on AI to help business owners understand and act on the numbers inside their books.

The Basics of Muse for Small Business

Muse is Meta's dedicated AI platform built specifically for small business owners.

Instead of bouncing between multiple apps and dashboards, Meta's vision is for owners to use Muse as a centralized hub. Through an AI assistant, users can interact with various tools, with QuickBooks being one of the core integrated services.

Once connected, you can ask Muse to execute supported QuickBooks functions or retrieve information directly from your account. According to Intuit, this includes creating and sending invoices, processing received payments, and asking targeted questions about overall business performance.

QuickBooks' Ongoing Shift Toward AI

If you follow small business accounting trends, this announcement isn't happening in a vacuum. QuickBooks has been leaning heavily into artificial intelligence all year.

Intuit continues to expand Intuit Intelligence, the native AI system embedded within its software. Current features cover conversational business intelligence, automated invoicing, transaction categorization, cash flow forecasting, and custom automations.

Users can already ask the system how cash flow shifted from month to month or how current expenses compare to the same period last year. Certain versions can even model the financial impact of potential business decisions—like adjusting prices, hiring a new employee, or taking on a recurring expense. Keep in mind that availability varies based on your specific QuickBooks plan, and some features are still in beta.

Why This AI Integration Matters for Your Business

The real takeaway isn't just that QuickBooks added another software integration. The core shift is how business owners are accessing their accounting information.

blocks.html:
Historically, answering a financial question meant knowing exactly which report to generate, which menu to navigate, or where a specific number was buried. Artificial intelligence is steadily removing those hurdles.

Rather than pulling multiple reports to investigate a trend, an owner might simply ask, "How did my cash flow change this quarter?" or request a new invoice without ever navigating through the accounting interface. This direct access makes financial data far more approachable for owners who aren't accountants.

Accurate Bookkeeping Remains the Foundation

There is one critical catch to these advancements: AI can only analyze the financial data you feed into it.

If your transactions are miscategorized, accounts sit unreconciled, personal and business expenses are mixed, or vital activity is missing entirely, the AI will generate answers based on flawed data.

QuickBooks highlights this reality directly. While its latest AI tools are built to automate routine bookkeeping tasks, Intuit explicitly recommends working alongside an accountant or bookkeeper when relying on automated bookkeeping services. This oversight becomes even more crucial when you ask AI to interpret your financial health rather than simply logging receipts.

AI Delivers Information, But Advisors Deliver Context

Imagine asking an AI tool if your business expenses went up this year.

QuickBooks can likely confirm the increase, calculate the exact difference, and isolate which categories saw the biggest jumps.

But that data alone doesn't answer the strategic questions.

Was that expense increase expected? Is it dragging down profitability? Do you need to adjust your pricing model? Does a major equipment purchase carry specific tax implications? Is your cash flow actually strong enough to support a new hire? Should you finalize a transaction before December 31, or hold off until next year?

Those nuanced questions require context—and that is exactly where a conversation with a dedicated tax professional or accountant provides irreplaceable value.

Navigating Your Evolving Accounting Tools

QuickBooks linking up with Meta's Muse proves that AI is rapidly becoming a standard piece of everyday small business financial management. While faster answers and automated admin work are great news for business owners, easier access to data makes accurate bookkeeping more critical than ever. AI surfaces the numbers, but ensuring they are correct and understanding what they mean for your strategy is a collaborative effort.

title: How the New Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Can Optimize Your K-12 Educational Giving
excerpt: Explore the upcoming IRC Section 25F tax credit starting in 2027. Learn how this federal incentive for K-12 scholarship donations interacts with state credits and traditional deductions to refine your tax strategy.
description: Understand the upcoming IRC Section 25F Federal Scholarship Tax Credit. Learn about the $1,700 cap, state offset rules, and carryforward provisions.

blocks.html:
Congress has introduced a new federal incentive designed for individuals who want to support K–12 education. Codified under IRC Section 25F, this provision establishes a nonrefundable federal income tax credit for qualified cash contributions made to approved scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) that fund scholarships for eligible elementary and secondary students. Designated as the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, this rule is designed to expand educational opportunities for children from low- and middle-income households by encouraging private donations that support K–12 learning.

For taxpayers, this upcoming provision represents a fundamental shift in how educational philanthropy interacts with tax planning. It is far more than a standard charitable-giving rule; it directly alters the tax outcome of your donation, depends heavily on state-level participation, and interacts dynamically with existing state credits and federal charitable deduction rules in ways that will shape your overall financial strategy.

The Strategic Intent Behind Section 25F

At a policy level, Section 25F is structured to direct private dollars toward scholarship programs that help students who might otherwise lack access to a diverse range of educational options. The law targets households with annual incomes at or below 300% of the area median gross income, and the student must also be eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. This income threshold ensures that the credit is aimed at families who, while not necessarily impoverished, encounter serious financial barriers when seeking educational alternatives for their children.

This program is a significant development because many taxpayers already make generous contributions to education-focused nonprofit organizations. Section 25F enhances the incentive for these actions by turning a portion of the gift into a direct federal tax credit rather than leaving the tax benefit solely to standard charitable deduction rules. This makes the program highly appealing to donors who want to support educational opportunities while maximizing their tax planning.

Effective Date: When to Plan for the Credit

It is important to note that this federal tax credit is not currently effective. This discussion serves as an early planning brief regarding a delayed provision enacted under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The credit becomes effective beginning in 2027, meaning contributions made post-2026 will qualify for the first credit claims on 2027 federal income tax returns.

How the Credit Operates in Practice

Under IRC Section 25F, individual taxpayers who are U.S. citizens or residents can claim a federal tax credit equal to the qualified cash contributions made during the tax year. The contribution must be in cash—which includes payments via check or credit card—and must be made to an approved scholarship-granting organization that utilizes the funds to distribute scholarships to eligible students. To qualify, these scholarships must cover approved educational expenses, including tuition, transportation, room and board fees, tutoring services, school supplies, and special needs assistance.

The annual credit is capped at $1,700 per taxpayer. This strict cap means that any contribution exceeding $1,700 will not generate an additional federal credit; the law functions as a donor incentive rather than a full reimbursement of every dollar contributed. While we await final clarification from the IRS, it is expected that the maximum credit allowed on a joint return will be capped at $1,700, rather than $3,400. Notably, this $1,700 limit is not subject to any phase-out thresholds based on the donor's income.

A qualifying contribution must be used to support students within the specific state where the SGO is officially registered and approved. Every state (as well as the District of Columbia) must choose to participate by providing the IRS with a registry of approved SGOs. Because of this requirement, state coordination is critical; this is not an automatic nationwide credit. However, donors are not required to reside in the same state as the SGO. For instance, a resident of California can contribute to an approved SGO in Florida and qualify for the federal credit, even if California chooses not to participate in the program.

Widening Educational Access for Families

The defining element of the Section 25F credit is its focus on student eligibility. To qualify for a scholarship funded by these contributions, a student must reside in a household with an income that does not exceed 300% of the area median gross income, and they must be eligible to attend a public K–12 school. This relatively broad threshold is intentionally designed to support families who are often overlooked by traditional financial aid programs—those who earn too much to qualify for low-income assistance but do not earn enough to comfortably absorb private tuition or specialized services.

By routing scholarship funds to this specific demographic, the statute aims to expand educational choice and help families secure learning environments that align with their children's needs. In practice, these scholarship dollars help cover critical expenses like tuition, mandatory fees, and other qualifying K–12 educational costs defined by law.
